summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, and diabetes was admitted with chest pain radiating to the back and bradycardia. Initial evaluation revealed severe hyperkalemia and a junctional rhythm, with peaked T waves on ECG. The chest pain did not respond to nitroglycerin and was concerning for cardiac ischemia, but echocardiogram showed preserved systolic function without new wall motion abnormalities. Dialysis was performed at the bedside, resulting in normalization of potassium and resolution of bradycardia. The chest pain improved and was no longer present at discharge. Contrast extravasation occurred during a CT scan, causing right hand swelling and pain; the hand surgery team evaluated and managed it conservatively. The patient was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged for hand surgery, nephrology, and cardiology, and instructed to resume outpatient dialysis and monitor for recurrent symptoms.
